items.readable_text:
Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw how to conduct a hypothesis test to check whether two means are equal for populations with equal variance. In this lesson, we will learn how to perform a hypothesis test, called an ANOVA test, to determine if the population means of three or more groups are equal.

Content:
Suppose we have [MATH: K] groups and [MATH: \mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots \mu_K] are the population means of each group.

Content:
Then, we can formulate the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K]
- [MATH: H_1{:}] There is at least one population mean that differs from the others.

Content:
The test statistic we will use is
[MATH: W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}},]
where

Content:
- [MATH: \text{MSW}] is the mean sum of squares within groups,
- [MATH: \text{MSB}] is the mean sum of squares between groups.

Content:
Intuitively, we can interpret [MATH: W] as follows:

Content:
- If [MATH: W] is large, then [MATH: \text{MSB}] is much greater than [MATH: \text{MSW}.] This means that the average variation between one group and another is larger than the average deviation within a group. If [MATH: W] exceeds some threshold value, we reject [MATH: H_0.]
- If [MATH: W] is small, then [MATH: \text{MSB}] is much smaller than [MATH: \text{MSW}.] This means that the average variation between groups is smaller than the average variation within groups. If [MATH: W] is smaller than some threshold value, we don't reject [MATH: H_0.]

Content:
The statistic [MATH: W] is called [MATH: F]-ratio because, as we will see, it follows a Fisher's [MATH: F]-distribution (provided certain assumptions hold).

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have a sample of size [MATH: n,] where the observations are divided into [MATH: K] groups. We want to determine whether the population mean varies by group.

Content:
In other words, we want to test the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K]
- [MATH: H_1{:}] There is at least one population mean that differs from the others,

Content:
where [MATH: \mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_K] are the population means of each group.

Content:
We've already introduced the [MATH: F]-ratio test statistic for this problem:
[MATH: W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}]

Content:
Now, we will discuss the distribution of [MATH: W.]

Content:
Let's assume that the data points are independent and follow a normal distribution with equal mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2{:}]
[MATH: X_{jk} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad j=1, 2, \ldots, n_k, \quad k=1, 2, \ldots, K]
where [MATH: n_k] is the size of the [MATH: k]th group.

Content:
Also, recall that
[MATH: \textrm{SST} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X})^2, \qquad
\text{SSW} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2, \qquad
\text{SSB} = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k (\overline{X}_k - \overline{X})^2.]

Content:
Given a sample of [MATH: n] independent normal random variables with variance [MATH: \sigma^2], for the sample variance [MATH: S^2,] we have
[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2(n-1).]

Content:
We can use this result to find the distribution of [MATH: \text{SST}/\sigma^2.] Since
[MATH: \textrm{SST} = (n-1)S^2]
it follows that
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{SST}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2(n-1).]

Content:
We can also apply this result to each group mean:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n_k-1), \quad k = 1, \ldots, K]
Moreover, the above sums are independent. Since each group variance contributes [MATH: (n_k - 1)] degrees of freedom, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\text{SSW}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n - K).]

Content:
It can be shown that [MATH: \text{SSB}] and [MATH: \text{SSW}] are independent. Therefore, since [MATH: \text{SST} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW},] we have that
[MATH: \text{SSB}/\sigma^2] follows a chi-squared distribution with [MATH: n-1 - (n-K) = K-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
Notice that our test statistic [MATH: W] is the ratio of two independent chi-squared random variables divided by their respective degrees of freedom:
[MATH: (((SSB)/(σ^{2})))/(((SSW)/(σ^{2}))) ⋅ (n − K)/(K − 1)|= (((SSB)/(σ^{2})))/(((SSW)/(σ^{2}))) ⋅ (n − K)/(K − 1); = (((SSB)/(K − 1)))/(((SSW)/(n − K))); = (MSB)/(MSW); = W]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: W] follows a Fisher's [MATH: F]-distribution with [MATH: \nu_1=K-1] and [MATH: \nu_2=n-K] degrees of freedom.

Content:
[MATH: W\sim F(K-1, n-K).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw how to conduct a hypothesis test to check whether two means are equal for populations with equal variance. In this lesson, we will learn how to perform a hypothesis test, called an ANOVA test, to determine if the population means of three or more groups are equal.

Content:
Suppose we have [MATH: K] groups and [MATH: \mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots \mu_K] are the population means of each group.

Content:
Then, we can formulate the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K]
- [MATH: H_1{:}] There is at least one population mean that differs from the others.

Content:
The test statistic we will use is
[MATH: W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}},]
where

Content:
- [MATH: \text{MSW}] is the mean sum of squares within groups,
- [MATH: \text{MSB}] is the mean sum of squares between groups.

Content:
Intuitively, we can interpret [MATH: W] as follows:

Content:
- If [MATH: W] is large, then [MATH: \text{MSB}] is much greater than [MATH: \text{MSW}.] This means that the average variation between one group and another is larger than the average deviation within a group. If [MATH: W] exceeds some threshold value, we reject [MATH: H_0.]
- If [MATH: W] is small, then [MATH: \text{MSB}] is much smaller than [MATH: \text{MSW}.] This means that the average variation between groups is smaller than the average variation within groups. If [MATH: W] is smaller than some threshold value, we don't reject [MATH: H_0.]

Content:
The statistic [MATH: W] is called [MATH: F]-ratio because, as we will see, it follows a Fisher's [MATH: F]-distribution (provided certain assumptions hold).

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The One-Factor ANOVA Table

Content:
It will be convenient to collect all the relevant statistics for this problem in a one-factor ANOVA table, shown below.

Content:
| Source | [MATH: \,\textrm{SS}\,] | [MATH: \,df\,] | [MATH: \,\textrm{MS}\,] | [MATH: \,F\,] |
| Between Groups | [MATH: \text{SSB}] | [MATH: K-1] | [MATH: \text{MSB}=\dfrac{\text{SSB}}{K-1}] | [MATH: \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}] |
| Within Groups | [MATH: \text{SSW}] | [MATH: n-K] | [MATH: \text{MSW}=\dfrac{\text{SSW}}{n-K}] | |
| Total | [MATH: \text{SST}] | [MATH: n-1] | | |

Content:
Recall that:

Content:
- [MATH: \text{SSW}] is the sum of squares within groups,
- [MATH: \text{SSB}] is the sum of squares between groups,
- [MATH: \text{SST}] is the total sum of squares, and [MATH: \text{SST}=\text{SSW}+\text{SSB},]
- [MATH: K] is the number of groups,
- [MATH: n] is the total number of sample elements.

Content:

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Distribution of the F-Ratio

Content:
Suppose we have a sample of size [MATH: n,] where the observations are divided into [MATH: K] groups. We want to determine whether the population mean varies by group.

Content:
In other words, we want to test the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0{:}\: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_K]
- [MATH: H_1{:}] There is at least one population mean that differs from the others,

Content:
where [MATH: \mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_K] are the population means of each group.

Content:
We've already introduced the [MATH: F]-ratio test statistic for this problem:
[MATH: W = \dfrac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}}]

Content:
Now, we will discuss the distribution of [MATH: W.]

Content:
Let's assume that the data points are independent and follow a normal distribution with equal mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2{:}]
[MATH: X_{jk} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad j=1, 2, \ldots, n_k, \quad k=1, 2, \ldots, K]
where [MATH: n_k] is the size of the [MATH: k]th group.

Content:
Also, recall that
[MATH: \textrm{SST} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X})^2, \qquad
\text{SSW} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} (X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2, \qquad
\text{SSB} = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k (\overline{X}_k - \overline{X})^2.]

Content:
Given a sample of [MATH: n] independent normal random variables with variance [MATH: \sigma^2], for the sample variance [MATH: S^2,] we have
[MATH: \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim\chi^2(n-1).]

Content:
We can use this result to find the distribution of [MATH: \text{SST}/\sigma^2.] Since
[MATH: \textrm{SST} = (n-1)S^2]
it follows that
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{SST}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2(n-1).]

Content:
We can also apply this result to each group mean:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n_k-1), \quad k = 1, \ldots, K]
Moreover, the above sums are independent. Since each group variance contributes [MATH: (n_k - 1)] degrees of freedom, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\text{SSW}}{\sigma^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}(X_{jk} - \overline{X}_k)^2 \sim \chi^2(n - K).]

Content:
It can be shown that [MATH: \text{SSB}] and [MATH: \text{SSW}] are independent. Therefore, since [MATH: \text{SST} = \text{SSB} + \text{SSW},] we have that
[MATH: \text{SSB}/\sigma^2] follows a chi-squared distribution with [MATH: n-1 - (n-K) = K-1] degrees of freedom.

Content:
Notice that our test statistic [MATH: W] is the ratio of two independent chi-squared random variables divided by their respective degrees of freedom:
[MATH: (((SSB)/(σ^{2})))/(((SSW)/(σ^{2}))) ⋅ (n − K)/(K − 1)|= (((SSB)/(σ^{2})))/(((SSW)/(σ^{2}))) ⋅ (n − K)/(K − 1); = (((SSB)/(K − 1)))/(((SSW)/(n − K))); = (MSB)/(MSW); = W]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: W] follows a Fisher's [MATH: F]-distribution with [MATH: \nu_1=K-1] and [MATH: \nu_2=n-K] degrees of freedom.

Content:
[MATH: W\sim F(K-1, n-K).]
